title: Deep in one: the Psalms
for: I want to pray the Psalms
subtitle: Ten sessions in the Bible's own prayer book: how its five books are arranged, how its poetry works, and how to pray its praise, lament, confession and curses with Christ.
intro: This track reads ten psalms closely and learns to pray them. Most of Scripture speaks to you. The Psalms give you words to speak back to God, and Athanasius, writing in the fourth century, said they work like a mirror in which a reader finds the movements of their own soul. They are a hundred and fifty poems gathered into five books, prayed by Israel for centuries before Jesus prayed them himself.

Each session opens one psalm in the Study Bible with its notes in plain words, and most also open it in Pray the Psalms, where you can pray it line by line. Read the psalm aloud before you begin, more than once if you can, because these are songs. The track takes the hard psalms as seriously as the beloved ones: lament, guilt, despair and the cry for vengeance are all in the book. Each session ends with a guide for a group.

about: This guide is for anyone leading a small group through Deep in one: the Psalms. The group meets ten times and reads and prays one psalm, or a short group of psalms, each time. It suits people who already pray and people who have never known how to start, because the Psalms give words to both. The leader's task is to keep the group in the text, and then to let the text become prayer.

Each person reads the psalm, its notes and the session before the group meets. The meeting reads the psalm aloud and talks it over, using the group guide for that session, which is gathered below in order with the page each session opens and the question it asks.

sections.title: The group
body: Four to ten people is a good size, small enough that everyone speaks. Meet for about seventy-five minutes, once a week, for ten meetings, and keep the end time you promised. A leader doesn't need to be a scholar or a fluent pray-er. A leader needs to have read the psalm and its notes, and to be willing to admit not knowing. Some groups find that praying the psalm aloud together at the end becomes the part people remember.

sections.title: The room
body: Sit in a circle round a table if you can, with the psalm open in front of everyone, in print or on a phone. The Psalms were sung, so read each one aloud, and try reading it in two halves of the room, one half taking the first line of each pair and the other the second. Make it plain at the first meeting that anyone may pass on any question, that what people say about their own lives stays in the room, and that no one has to pray aloud.

sections.title: The order of a meeting
body: About seventy-five minutes, in this order. Keep to the times loosely and to the end time strictly.
steps: Ten minutes: the opening question, once round the circle. Anyone may pass.
Ten minutes: read the psalm aloud twice, the second time slowly, in two voices if the group is willing.
Thirty-five minutes: the three questions to talk over, in order. Ask where each answer is in the psalm.
Five minutes: one person reads the verse to keep, and the group says what it noticed in it.
Ten minutes: the prayer prompt, in your own words, or the psalm itself prayed aloud together.
Five minutes: name the next psalm and the page its session opens, and say when you will meet.

sections.title: When a hard question comes
body: The Psalms raise hard questions: a psalm that ends in darkness, a prayer that asks God to strike an enemy, a verse about infants and rocks. When the group reaches one, read the note on it together before anyone answers. Say plainly where Christians have read a psalm in more than one way, give each reading its strongest form, and don't hurry to make the psalm comfortable. If no one knows, write the question down and bring it back the next week.

Some people will ask whether God really wants to hear anger, doubt or a cry for revenge. The Psalms answer that he has put such prayers in his own book. Welcome the question, and let the psalm show how those prayers are brought to God rather than acted out. Treating honesty as disloyalty ends the conversation, and the Psalter is the most honest book of prayer there is.

sections.title: When someone is hurting
body: The Psalms are full of people in trouble: sleepless, accused, ashamed, far from home, sure God has forgotten them. Someone in the group will find their own life in a psalm, and it may surprise them. When that happens, stop the discussion and listen. Thank the person for saying it, don't explain their suffering for them, and don't hurry them to the hopeful verse at the end. Ask whether they would like the group to go on or to pause, and speak with them on their own afterwards.

Never use a psalm to tell someone how they ought to feel, or to suggest that their sorrow shows a lack of faith; the Psalter itself refuses that. If someone says that a partner, a leader or anyone else is harming them or a child, take it seriously and don't promise to keep it secret.

sections.title: When to point someone to Find Help
body: Point someone to Find Help when what they carry has become too heavy to set down: grief or low mood that has taken their sleep or appetite for weeks, fear or guilt that will not let them rest, harm done to them at home or in a church, or any sign that they no longer want to be alive. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn, and its lines for help right now are open day and night. If anyone is in danger now, call your local emergency number. A leader is a friend in that moment, not a counsellor, and the kindest thing is often to stay with the person while they make the first call.

sessions.title: Psalm 1 and the two ways
teaching: The Psalter is not a loose pile of songs. It is a book of five books, and each of the first four closes with a burst of praise: at the end of Psalms 41, 72, 89 and 106. The fifth book closes with five psalms of nothing but praise, the last of them ending the whole collection. An old Jewish commentary on the Psalms compares the five books of psalms to the five books of Moses, and the comparison helps. These are prayers, but they are also instruction, a way of being formed by God's word as you pray it.

That is why the book opens as it does. Psalm 1 isn't a prayer at all. It is a door, and it sets two ways in front of you. One person delights in the law of the LORD and meditates on it day and night, and is like a tree planted by streams of water. The other is like chaff the wind drives off. The psalm doesn't tell you to try harder. It tells you where to put your roots, and it promises that the LORD watches over the way of the person whose roots are there.

open.label: Psalm 1, passage by passage
open.why: The two ways, the tree and the chaff, explained in plain words, with what it means that the whole Psalter begins here.

also.label: The Psalms in the Study Bible
also.why: Who wrote the Psalms and when, how the five books are arranged, the kinds of psalm, and where to begin reading.

also.label: Psalms: the prayer book of the Bible
also.why: The whole book in seven pictures: a gateway, five books and a last Hallelujah, lament, praise, and the prayers Jesus prayed.

also.label: Pray Psalm 1
also.why: Psalm 1 set out to pray line by line, with a short word on what kind of psalm it is and when to pray it.

sessions.question: Psalm 1 says the person who flourishes is the one whose roots go down into God's word. Where are your roots going down now?
sessions.do: Read Psalm 1 aloud every morning this week. On the last day, write down one thing in the week that drew you toward the tree and one that drew you toward the chaff.

verse.text: He is like a tree planted by streams of water, yielding its fruit in season, whose leaf does not wither, and who prospers in all he does.

group.open: Is there a psalm you have known all your life, or a line from one you remember? Where did you first hear it?
discuss: The Psalter begins with instruction rather than prayer. What does that tell you about how the book means to be used?
The tree doesn't make itself fruitful. It is planted by water. What would that look like in an ordinary week?
The psalm sets out only two ways. Is that too simple for real life, or does it see something we prefer not to see?
group.pray: Give thanks for God's word, and ask in your own words that each person in the group would be rooted by its streams in the weeks of this track.

sessions.title: Psalm 2 and the king
teaching: Psalm 1 and Psalm 2 stand together at the door of the book. Psalm 1 begins with the person who is blessed and Psalm 2 ends with all who take refuge in the LORD, and between them they name the two things the Psalter is about: God's word and God's king. Psalm 2 opens on the nations in uproar: “Why do the nations rage and the peoples plot in vain?” (Psalm 2:1). The kings of the earth set themselves against the LORD and his anointed one, and heaven laughs. God has set his king on Zion and calls him his Son.

Many scholars think Israel sang this psalm when a new king was crowned, and as the kings failed it became a hope for a king still to come. The first Christians heard it fulfilled in Jesus. When they were threatened, they prayed Psalm 2 aloud (Acts 4:25-26), and Hebrews opens its argument with the words to the Son (Hebrews 1:5). This is the first key to how Christians pray the Psalms. Many of them are the prayers of the king, and Jesus is the king who prayed them. When you pray them, you pray with him.

open.label: Psalm 2, passage by passage
open.why: The raging nations, the king on Zion and the hard line about kissing the Son, explained in plain words with the choices translators make.

also.label: The king
also.why: Seven pictures following one crown through the Bible, from a shepherd boy to the promise to David to a King on a cross.

also.label: The Messiah, in the Study Bible
also.why: What the Old Testament hoped for in an anointed king, and how the New Testament reads that hope in Jesus.

sessions.question: Psalm 2 says the nations rage and God is not anxious about it. What would change in you if you believed that this week?
sessions.do: Read Psalm 2, then Acts 4:23-31, where the church prays it under threat. Write down what the believers ask for, and what they do not ask for.

verse.text: Kiss the Son, lest He be angry and you perish in your rebellion, when His wrath ignites in an instant. Blessed are all who take refuge in Him.

group.open: What news story this year made you most uneasy about the world?
discuss: The psalm pictures heaven laughing at the plots of kings. Is that comforting or unsettling to you, and why?
The early church prayed this psalm when it was threatened. What did they find in it for their situation?
If Jesus is the king these psalms speak of, how does that change who is speaking when you pray them?
group.pray: Pray for the nations and their rulers by name, including your own, and give thanks that the world's uproar is not the last word.

sessions.title: Psalm 8 and how Hebrew poetry works
teaching: Hebrew poetry doesn't rhyme sounds. It rhymes thoughts. One line says something and the next says it again, or sharpens it, or answers it. Robert Lowth named this parallelism in his Oxford lectures of 1753, and once you see it you can't stop seeing it. Psalm 8 shows it clearly: “what is man that You are mindful of him, or the son of man that You care for him?” (Psalm 8:4). The second line is not a new subject. It presses the first one further, from being remembered to being cared for.

The psalm begins and ends with the same line about the majesty of God's name, and between them it looks up at the night sky and then down at us. Next to the moon and stars a human being looks tiny, and yet God has crowned us with glory and honour and given us rule over his works. Hebrews reads this psalm of Jesus, the man who was made a little lower than the angels for a while and is now crowned (Hebrews 2:9). The glory Psalm 8 gives to humankind, Christ wears first.

open.label: Psalm 8, passage by passage
open.why: The night sky, the question about humankind and the crown of glory, explained in plain words with how Hebrews reads the psalm.

also.label: Reading Hebrew poetry
also.why: How Hebrew poetry works: parallelism, terseness and imagery, the kinds of psalm, how the Psalter is arranged, and the headings explained.

also.label: Pray Psalm 8
also.why: Psalm 8 set out to pray line by line, best prayed outside at night, under the sky it describes.

sessions.question: Psalm 8 holds together how small you are and how much honour God gives you. Which of the two do you find harder to believe?
sessions.do: Go outside on a clear night this week and read Psalm 8 under the sky. Then mark each pair of lines in it and write down what the second line adds to the first.

verse.text: When I behold Your heavens, the work of Your fingers, the moon and the stars, which You have set in place— what is man that You are mindful of him, or the son of man that You care for him?

group.open: Where have you been when you felt smallest under the sky?
discuss: Read the psalm in two voices, one person to each line of a pair. What did you hear that you missed reading alone?
The psalm moves from God's majesty to human honour and back. Why do you think it begins and ends in the same place?
Hebrews reads Psalm 8 of Jesus. How does that change what it means for us to be crowned with glory?
group.pray: Spend a minute in silence on the size and order of what God has made, and then give thanks in your own words that he is mindful of each person in the room.

sessions.title: Psalm 13 and lament
teaching: The largest group of psalms is not praise. It is lament, the prayer of someone in trouble who brings it straight to God. Psalm 13 is one of the shortest, and it shows the whole shape in six verses. It begins with a complaint, asking how long four times over: “How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever? How long will You hide Your face from me?” (Psalm 13:1). Then it asks for help, plainly and urgently. Then, without any change in the situation that the psalm reports, it turns to trust and to song.

Lament is not the opposite of faith. It is faith that refuses to pretend. Many churches sing almost nothing but praise, and people in pain conclude that their sorrow has no place in worship. The Psalter disagrees, and it gives more room to lament than to anything else. Notice where the turn comes in Psalm 13. It doesn't come from feeling better. It comes from remembering God's loving devotion, and that is where a lament can take you when nothing else has changed.

open.label: Psalm 13, passage by passage
open.why: How long, O LORD, and the turn to trust, explained in plain words, with what the psalm does and does not promise.

also.label: Pray Psalm 13
also.why: Psalm 13 set out to pray line by line, for the days when the only honest prayer is how long.

also.label: How to practise lament
also.why: The shape of a lament, step by step, and how to write one of your own when you can't find the words.

also.label: Lament: a Bible study on praying your pain
also.why: A longer study of lament through the Bible, for a group or alone, when one session on it is not enough.

sessions.question: If you began a prayer to God with How long, what would come after those two words?
sessions.do: Write a lament of your own in four parts, following Psalm 13: a complaint, a request, a reason to trust, and a promise to praise. Keep it honest, even if the last part is only one line.

verse.text: But I have trusted in Your loving devotion; my heart will rejoice in Your salvation. I will sing to the LORD, for He has been good to me.

care: If ‘sorrow in my heart each day’ (verse 2) is your life now, please do not carry it alone. Tell someone you trust: a doctor, a pastor or a friend. If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: When you were growing up, was it acceptable to be sad in front of others? How did that shape you?
discuss: The psalmist asks God how long four times. Does it surprise you that such a prayer is in the Bible? Why?
The turn to trust comes before anything changes. What makes that possible, according to the psalm?
Why do you think lament is so rare in the songs many churches sing? What is lost when it is missing?
group.pray: Let anyone who wishes bring a how long of their own to God aloud or in silence, and then pray together for those who are waiting.

sessions.title: Psalm 23
teaching: Psalm 23 is so familiar that it is hard to hear. It is a psalm of trust, and it is built on two pictures. In the first God is a shepherd, and David, who had been one, knew what that meant: a shepherd finds grass and water, leads by safe paths, walks in front into the dark ravine and carries a rod against wolves and a staff for strays. In the second God is a host who spreads a table in front of the guest's enemies and fills the cup to overflowing.

Notice where the psalm turns. It speaks about the LORD in the third person until the valley, and in the valley it starts speaking to him: “for You are with me” (Psalm 23:4). The darkest place is where the prayer becomes most personal. The psalm doesn't promise there will be no valley. It promises company in it. Jesus called himself the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11), and Christians have prayed this psalm at deathbeds and gravesides for centuries for that reason.

open.label: Psalm 23, passage by passage
open.why: The shepherd, the right paths, the valley, the rod and staff, the table and the house, explained in plain words.

also.label: Psalm 23: the LORD is my shepherd
also.why: The psalm read line by line in seven pictures, as the Study Bible's notes read it, from green grass to the house at the end.

also.label: Pray Psalm 23
also.why: Psalm 23 set out to pray line by line, slowly enough to hear words you may have known all your life.

sessions.question: Psalm 23 begins speaking to God only in the valley. Where is your valley now, and what would it mean to speak to him there?
sessions.do: Pray Psalm 23 slowly each night this week, stopping at the line that holds you longest. On the last night, write that line down and say why it held you.

verse.text: Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for You are with me; Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me.

care: If you are grieving, this psalm does not ask you to feel calm. Read it slowly, and let the shepherd be with you in the valley you are in. Grief is not a failure of faith. If your grief has become too heavy to carry, please tell someone you trust, a pastor, a friend or a doctor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Where have you heard Psalm 23 read aloud, and what was happening at the time?
discuss: The psalm shifts from about God to to God in the valley. Why do you think it happens there?
A table spread in front of enemies is a strange picture of peace. What do you make of it?
Jesus called himself the good shepherd. How does that change the way you hear this psalm?
group.pray: Pray for anyone you know who is walking through a dark valley now, by name, and give thanks for the shepherd who walks in front.

sessions.title: Psalm 51 and confession
teaching: Psalm 51 carries a heading that sets it after the worst thing David did: when Nathan the prophet came to him, after he had taken Bathsheba and arranged her husband's death (2 Samuel 11 to 12). It is the church's great psalm of confession. It begins with God's character before it mentions sin: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to Your loving devotion” (Psalm 51:1). Then it names the wrong with no excuse and no softening, and asks for more than pardon. It asks for a clean heart, a new spirit, and the joy of salvation given back.

This psalm also guards against two mistakes. One is to think confession is only a feeling of being bad; David asks to be washed and to be made new. The other is to read a powerful man's confession as if it settled his debt to the people he harmed. Bathsheba was wronged and Uriah was killed, and the notes on this psalm say so plainly. Christians have prayed Psalm 51 for centuries, in the liturgies of Lent and in private, because it teaches the shape of repentance: God first, the wrong named, a new heart asked for.

open.label: Psalm 51, passage by passage
open.why: David's confession after Nathan came to him, explained in plain words, with care for Bathsheba and anyone harmed by someone with power.

also.label: Repentance, in the Study Bible
also.why: What the whole Bible means by repentance, a turning of the whole person, and how it differs from remorse alone.

also.label: How to confess sin and walk in repentance
also.why: Practical steps for confession before God and, where it is right, before the people wronged, without despair or excuse.

also.label: Pray Psalm 51
also.why: Psalm 51 set out to pray line by line, for the times when you know what you have done.

sessions.question: Psalm 51 asks for a clean heart, not just a clean record. What is the difference in your own life?
sessions.do: Read Psalm 51 slowly and underline every request David makes. Then spend ten quiet minutes naming before God one wrong you have excused, using the psalm's words where your own run out.

verse.text: Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me.

care: Sometimes guilt that will not lift needs more than a Bible verse. It can be part of anxiety, depression or a habit of the mind that keeps returning to the same fear. That is not a failure of faith. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor or a doctor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

If you have been harmed by someone with power over you, hear this too. What was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. The Bible did not blame Bathsheba, and it does not blame you. Please tell someone you trust. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Who taught you how to say sorry, and how did they teach it?
discuss: David appeals to God's loving devotion before he names his sin. Why does the order matter?
The psalm asks for a new heart and a willing spirit. What is confession for, if it is more than relief?
David's confession is real, and Bathsheba and Uriah were still wronged. How should repentance face the people harmed?
group.pray: Give a few minutes of silence for each person to confess privately, and then give thanks together for the God whose mercy comes first.

sessions.title: Psalms 42 and 43, the downcast soul
teaching: Psalms 42 and 43 belong together. They share a refrain that comes three times, and some Hebrew manuscripts copy them as one psalm. The speaker is far from the temple, mocked by people who ask where his God is, and longing for God the way a deer longs for water. The refrain is a man talking to himself: “Why are you downcast, O my soul? Why the unease within me? Put your hope in God” (Psalm 42:5). He doesn't deny how low he is. He argues with it.

This is one of the most honest pictures of low spirits in the Bible, and it gives no single cure. It doesn't say why he is downcast, and it doesn't say the feeling lifted. What it shows is a person who keeps remembering, keeps asking, and keeps telling his own soul to hope, three times over. Some readers find that the refrain becomes their own prayer for a season. Others need a doctor as well as the psalm, and that is no failure of faith. The psalm leaves room for both.

open.label: Psalm 42, passage by passage
open.why: The thirsting deer, the mocking question and the refrain, explained in plain words, with care for anyone who is low now.

also.label: Pray Psalm 43
also.why: The second half of the poem set out to pray line by line, ending in the refrain one last time.

also.label: Is anxiety a spiritual failure?
also.why: Why Scripture never treats distress as proof of weak faith, and how prayer and medical care belong together.

sessions.question: The psalmist speaks to his own soul instead of only listening to it. What would you say to yours this week?
sessions.do: Read Psalms 42 and 43 together as one poem. Write out the refrain each time it appears, and between them note one thing the speaker remembers or asks for.

verse.text: Why are you downcast, O my soul? Why the unease within me? Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise Him, my Savior and my God.

care: No one should read this psalm and decide what is wrong with someone else. It does not say why he is low, and it gives no single cure. If ‘my tears have been my food both day and night’ is true of you now, please do not carry it alone. Tell someone you trust: a doctor, a pastor or a friend. If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: What do you do when you feel low for no reason you can name?
discuss: The psalmist is mocked with the question, Where is your God? Have you ever heard that question, from others or from yourself?
The refrain is a man arguing with his own soul. How is that different from simply cheering yourself up?
The poem never says the feeling lifted. Why might that be a comfort rather than a disappointment?
group.pray: Pray for anyone in the group or beyond it whose soul is downcast now, gently and by name if they wish, and hold them before God without hurrying them.

sessions.title: A hard psalm: Psalm 137
teaching: Psalm 137 begins as one of the most beautiful laments in the Bible: “By the rivers of Babylon we sat and wept when we remembered Zion” (Psalm 137:1). The exiles hang up their harps, and their captors mock them by asking for a song. Then it ends with a line no one can read easily, a blessing on whoever dashes Babylon's infants against the rocks. Don't skip it, and don't explain it away. These are the words of people who had watched their city burned and their own children killed, and they are in Scripture.

Christians have read the cursing psalms in more than one way. Some see in them a cry for justice handed to God instead of taken by the sufferer's own hand, which is what Paul asks of believers (Romans 12:19). Dietrich Bonhoeffer argued that Christians pray them through Christ, who took God's judgment on himself and prayed for his enemies from the cross. Others say plainly that the psalm shows us what rage sounds like, not what we should wish for. Each reading takes the psalm seriously. None of them makes it comfortable.

open.label: Psalm 137, passage by passage
open.why: The rivers of Babylon, the silent harps and the terrible last verse, explained in plain words with the ways Christians have read it.

also.label: Hard passages
also.why: Every hard passage the notes take up, book by book. In the Psalms, look for the cursing psalms, Psalm 109 among them.

also.label: Exile and coming home
also.why: Seven pictures of God's people far from home and brought back, from the garden gate to Babylon to the city at the end.

also.label: Pray Psalm 137
also.why: Psalm 137 set out to pray line by line, with a word on how to bring rage to God rather than act it out.

sessions.question: Psalm 137 brings rage to God instead of acting on it. What anger are you carrying that you have never said to him?
sessions.do: Read Psalm 137, then Psalm 109 and the notes on both. Write down what each speaker has suffered, and then read Romans 12:17-21 and note what Paul asks of believers.

verse.text: How can we sing a song of the LORD in a foreign land?

care: If you carry rage at what was done to you, or to someone you love, this psalm shows that God can hear even that. Your rage is heard. Hand it to God rather than to your own hands. Tell a trusted person: a pastor, a friend, a counsellor. If you are in danger, or fear you might hurt someone, get help today. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: What is something you were taught never to say in a prayer?
discuss: The first verses of Psalm 137 are loved and the last verse is skipped. What do we lose when we read only the first part?
Which of the Christian readings of the cursing psalms do you find most honest, and why?
Jesus prayed for his enemies from the cross. Can a person pray Psalm 137 and still follow him? How?
group.pray: Bring to God in silence any anger each of you carries against someone who has done harm, and ask him to take the judgment out of your hands.

sessions.title: Psalm 90 and our days
teaching: Psalm 90 is the only psalm headed as a prayer of Moses, and it opens the fourth book of the Psalter, just after Psalm 89 has mourned a fallen king. With the throne empty, the book reaches back past David to Moses and to a God older than the mountains: “Lord, You have been our dwelling place through all generations” (Psalm 90:1). Then it sets the shortness of a human life beside that eternity without flinching. Seventy years, eighty if we are strong, and they quickly pass, and we fly away.

The psalm doesn't turn that fact into despair or into a slogan. It turns it into a request: teach us to number our days, that we may present a heart of wisdom. Knowing your life is short is meant to make you wise, not frantic. And the psalm ends by asking God to establish the work of our hands, twice over, as if it knows how little of what we build outlasts us without him. Christians have read Psalm 90 at funerals for generations, because it tells the truth about time and still dares to ask for joy.

open.label: Psalm 90, passage by passage
open.why: The dwelling place, the thousand years, the seventy years and the work of our hands, explained in plain words with care for the grieving.

also.label: Pray Psalm 90
also.why: Psalm 90 set out to pray line by line, for birthdays, new years, funerals and any day you feel time passing.

also.label: Hope, in the Study Bible
also.why: What the whole Bible means by hope, from the Psalms' longing to the resurrection, and why it is more than optimism.

sessions.question: What would change in how you spend this week if you numbered your days the way Psalm 90 asks?
sessions.do: Write down roughly how many years you have lived and how many you might have left. Then read Psalm 90 and write one thing you want God to establish of the work of your hands.

verse.text: So teach us to number our days, that we may present a heart of wisdom.

care: Paul wrote that Christians do grieve, but “not grieve like the rest, who are without hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Grief is not a lack of faith. If your grief feels too heavy to carry, please tell someone you trust: a pastor, a friend or a doctor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: At what age did you first realise that life is short? What made you see it?
discuss: The psalm puts God's eternity and our brief lives side by side. Does that make you feel small, safe, or both?
Numbering our days is meant to make us wise. What is the difference between wisdom and worry about time?
The psalm asks twice for the work of our hands to be established. What work of yours do you most want to last?
group.pray: Give thanks for the years each person has been given, pray for anyone grieving a life that ended, and ask God to establish the work of your hands.

sessions.title: Psalms 145 to 150, the last praise
teaching: The Hebrew name of the whole book means praises, and Psalm 145 is the only psalm whose own heading calls it a psalm of praise. It is an acrostic, each line beginning with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, praise from A to Z. Then the book ends with five psalms, 146 to 150, each of which begins and ends with Hallelujah, praise the LORD. The laments have not been forgotten. The book has carried them all the way through, and it ends here because that is where the whole story is going.

This is how the church has prayed the Psalms. Benedict's Rule had monks pray all hundred and fifty every week. Augustine heard in them the voice of the whole Christ, head and body, so that Jesus prays them with his people and his people pray them in him. Bonhoeffer called the Psalter the prayer book of the Bible and said Christians learn to pray by praying it. You have read ten psalms. There are a hundred and forty more, and the next track in this program, on Paul's letter to the Romans, shows the gospel these prayers were waiting for.

sessions.question: The Psalter ends in praise after a hundred and fifty psalms of every kind. What would it take for your praise to hold all you have lived?
sessions.do: Choose one psalm a day for the next month, beginning with Psalm 146, and pray it aloud in Pray the Psalms. When you reach a lament on a good day, pray it for someone who needs it.
